articles.title: Why did humans' brains surpass chimps'? A tiny foe might help explain it
articles.text:
Why did humans' brains surpass chimps'? A tiny foe might help explain it
Skip to content
Subscribe today
Every print subscription comes with full digital access
Subscribe Now
By Jake Buehler
19 hours ago
Share this:
Share
Share via email (Opens in new window)
Email
Share on Facebook (Opens in new window)
Facebook
Share on Reddit (Opens in new window)
Reddit
Share on X (Opens in new window)
Print (Opens in new window)
Print
Viruses may be minuscule, but one could have influenced major differences between human and chimpanzee brains.
Millions of years ago, a virus left DNA behind in an African ape’s genome, and the genetic material stuck around in modern day chimps. Those ghosts of infections past appear to influence genes involved in neuron development, which may help explain how human and chimp brains ended up so different, researchers report October 23 in Science Advances.
Compared with the brains of their chimpanzee kin, human brains are three times larger and more cognitively powerful. Yet “most of their protein-making genes are very similar,” says Johan Jakobsson, a neuroscientist at Lund University in Sweden. In the absence of large differences in the genetic code, Jakobsson and his colleagues decided to look at the parts of the human and chimp genome that control when and where genes are turned on or off.
Changes in gene regulation can come from viruses. Some viruses called retroviruses insert their own DNA into their hosts’ genomes to command host cells to build more viruses. But those parasitic bits of DNA can linger long after an infection. If this happens in reproductive cells, the viral DNA gets passed down with the host’s DNA.
These leftover bits, called endogenous retroviruses, no longer code for the production of infectious viruses, but they can have a big impact on the host’s biology — especially if they make copies of themselves across the genome. And they have. Such viral remnants make up at least 8 percent of the genomes of humans and chimps alike. More generally, these DNA leftovers have been linked with some major evolutionary events, such as the evolution of the mammalian placenta.
Jakobsson and his colleagues focused on a particular viral vestige in chimps. The holdover came from an infection in an ancestral African ape somewhere between 5 million and 7 million years ago. In chimpanzees, the viral DNA had stuck itself into the genome at 158 different locations. However, it is curiously absent in humans. It’s still unknown why.
The researchers wanted to know how that exact pathogen footprint might affect chimpanzees’ brains compared with those of humans. Working with chimpanzee stem cells, they removed the viral DNA using CRISPR, a gene editing technology that allows for precise, targeted cuts in DNA. Once the viral DNA was gone, a nearby gene called LINC00662 — normally silenced in chimpanzees — turned on, making RNA the team could detect. This matches the normal condition in human brain cells, in which LINC00662 is active. The team also used CRISPR to shut off LINC00662 in the human cells, matching the silenced condition seen in chimpanzees.
When LINC00662 was active in chimp or human cells, the researchers noticed activity boosts to other genes that may be important to brain development — such as genes involved in the development and maturation of neurons and in making new neural connections. It’s not yet clear exactly how the viral DNA’s shutdown of this brain gene network affected the biology of chimpanzee brains. However, this genetic difference may have contributed to a divergence in how human and chimpanzee brains evolved, Jakobsson says. “Our findings show one way an ancient viral [DNA] insertion could create a lasting difference in how a gene is regulated in humans and chimpanzees,” Jakobsson says. Other genetic and environmental changes could be involved in the puzzle as well, he says.
Researchers have previously looked to single letter swaps in DNA to help explain how humans and chimp brains drifted apart in their evolution. But the new study highlights that creatures can rack up genome changes in other ways, says Giorgia Modenini, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Padua in Italy who was not involved with this research.
The researchers do a convincing job of showing that these particular viral leftovers influence developmental differences between human and chimp neurons, says Ravinder Kanda, an evolutionary geneticist at Oxford Brookes University in Oxford, England. “They’ve proved that absolutely. How far that goes, I don’t think we can quite say yet.”
It could be that other controls on genes’ activity are also involved or that this particular ancient lever-puller may represent just a sliver of the viral holdovers that have shaped brain development, Kanda says. “I think there are many, many more retroviruses to be discovered, and at the moment we’ve only touched the tip of the iceberg.”

articles.title: Eating too much sugar on antibiotics could squash helpful gut bacteria
articles.text:
Eating too much sugar on antibiotics could squash helpful gut bacteria
Skip to content
Subscribe today

By Mariella Careaga
21 hours ago
Share this:
Share
Share via email (Opens in new window)
Email
Share on Facebook (Opens in new window)
Facebook
Share on Reddit (Opens in new window)
Reddit
Share on X (Opens in new window)
Print (Opens in new window)
Print
While a spoonful of sugar might help us gulp down a bitter-tasting antibiotic, it also may increase the damage that these drugs cause to the gut microbes.
In patients being treated for blood cancers, eating sugary items during antibiotic treatment was linked to a greater reduction in gut bacteria diversity than taking the antibiotics alone. The combination was also tied to the growth of gut bacteria associated with hard-to-treat infections, researchers report September 30 in Nature.
Cancer patients have lots of variation in their diets and take medications that can damage their microbiome. So, these patients provide a unique opportunity to study dramatic gut changes “that we believe are also relevant in the healthy context,” says Jonas Schluter, a microbiologist at NYU Langone Health.
Previous evidence separately suggested that antibiotics and sugars can disrupt the gut microbiome. But their combined effects, particularly in people at greater risk of infection, was unclear.
Researchers closely tracked more than 9,000 meals eaten by 173 people hospitalized in a treatment center to undergo blood-forming stem cell transplants. “Diet records are one of the biggest black boxes in a lot of diet microbiome studies,” since meals are often self-reported, says Tiffany Weir, a microbiologist at Colorado State University in Fort Collins, who was not involved in the research.
Standardized hospital meals allowed researchers to measure multiple days’ worth of food intake down to the gram, then compare the amounts of various nutrients eaten with bacterial diversity data obtained from stool samples.
For every additional 100 grams of sugar (the equivalent of 2.5 cans of Coke) that patients on antibiotics ate in the two days before sampling, the team found a 24 percent decrease in bacterial diversity. Consuming sweets and sugary beverages during antibiotic treatment was also associated with blooms of Enterococcus bacteria, which can be drug-resistant and are linked to difficult-to-treat infections associated with longer hospital stays and higher mortality.
“Some bacteria, sometimes, survive antibiotics, or perhaps more dangerously, they are resistant to [them],” Schluter says. By giving these bacteria the “universal resource for life, which is simple sugars, we are exacerbating their dominance. It’s almost like burning down the rainforest with a lot of fire, and then trying to extinguish the flames by putting in more petrol.”
The researchers also exposed mice on standard or sucrose-rich diets to a single dose of antibiotics. They found that the sugar exacerbated the enterococcal abundance after antibiotic exposure.
“Reducing sugar intake could be another way for patients to support their gut microbiome during antibiotic treatment,” says Sarah Berry, a nutrition scientist at King’s College London who was not involved in the study. Still, more research is needed to determine whether the findings apply to anyone on these drugs.
Schluter hopes that further studies and clinical trials can help uncover more about the exact relationship between sugar, antibiotics and the gut microbiome.
“You need to take antibiotics to fight infections, but you should also be aware that they have side effects to the microbiome,” Schluter says. “Now, we need to find strategies to mitigate this damage.”

Electric stoves could help people with asthma breathe easier

Print
For people with asthma, switching from a gas stove to an electric one might be a breath of fresh air. The combustion that creates the flame of a gas stove or oven releases pollutants, including nitrogen dioxide, which can trigger asthma symptoms. After a research-backed electric stove replacement, people reported more symptom relief than is often achieved with asthma medications.
“We were really surprised at how large the benefit was,” says Ashwini Sehgal, a clinician who studies community health at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland. With funding from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency during the Biden administration, Sehgal and colleagues spearheaded a project to install electric stoves in Cleveland households that had at least one person with asthma.
Eighty-five participants who had poorly controlled asthma were given a questionnaire a few months after the switch. They reported symptom improvement that was roughly two to three times as large as what’s typical with medication. Those with the worst symptoms saw the biggest improvement. Participants also reported fewer emergency room or hospital visits and said they missed work or school less often.
One 38-year-old woman told Sehgal’s team that whenever she cooked on her gas stove, she felt like her throat was closing. But the sensation disappeared after she switched to electric. Another participant, a 36-year-old man, found it difficult to walk uphill and play with his kids. With the stove swap, “he described how much better he felt as ‘magical,’ ” Sehgal says.
While heating, steaming or frying on a gas stovetop, nearby NO2 levels can skyrocket, reaching hundreds of parts per billion. That’s much higher than the EPA’s one-hour outdoor air quality standard of 100 parts per billion. NO2 exposure is linked to increased asthma symptoms. For example, research in children has found the pollutant can boost wheezing, coughing and asthma attacks.
The project was initially funded to follow 1,200 households for 12 months. But the Trump administration terminated the EPA’s Community Change Grants early, which drastically reduced the number of study participants. Yet even with this small group, the symptom improvement was significant.
The decision to replace a gas stove “depends on how much you are struggling with your own illness,” says environmental epidemiologist Carrie Breton of WashU Bursky School of Public Health in St. Louis. As a trial run, Sehgal suggests using an electric hot plate and a toaster oven to see if keeping the gas stove off helps improve symptoms.
If a stove swap isn’t in the budget, reducing NO2 exposure is still worthwhile, says pulmonologist Laura Paulin of Dartmouth Health. She recommends using kitchen ventilation, either via an exhaust hood that vents to the outside or an open window. A HEPA filter with a carbon insert can trap NO2 to decrease airborne concentrations. And try to keep children with asthma out of the kitchen when the stove is on, Paulin says. “It is a daunting task to replace a stove, but it doesn’t have to be an all-or-nothing thing.”
For researchers, the next step would be to measure lung function before and after a stove switch, Breton says. It would also be helpful to account for more factors, such as seasonal effects. “Many things can trigger people’s asthma,” Paulin says. Researchers could do a randomized trial in which some people get the electric stove right away while others wait for six months, Sehgal says, to allow time for comparison.
If electric stoves continue to be linked with fewer trips to the emergency room, fewer hospitalizations and better symptom control than medication can provide, “health insurance companies should consider paying for or subsidizing” stove swaps, Sehgal says. “If it truly works this well,” Breton says, “it’s got a bigger bang for your buck.”

articles.text:
A nanoparticle revealed the tiny impact of a single gas atom
Skip to content

It’s one of gentlest caresses imaginable: the touch of a single atom of gas. Now, scientists have measured its impact.
A levitating nanoparticle jiggled when hit by individual gas atoms or molecules in a nearly empty vacuum chamber, scientists report in the October 23 Physical Review Letters.
The force exerted by a gas is usually the result of many atoms or molecules bouncing around all at once: Think of the air inside a balloon keeping it inflated. But even an individual atom can exert a tiny force. To detect that force, researchers used a laser to levitate a glass sphere, just 100 nanometers across and weighing about a quadrillionth of a gram, inside a vacuum chamber. Then, the researchers added small amounts of a heavy gas, either krypton, xenon or sulfur hexafluoride. The first two are gases made up of atoms, while the third consists of molecules.
The nanosphere was about 10 million times as massive as an individual gas particle, making the impact extremely difficult to detect. But, by monitoring the laser light that reflected from the sphere, the researchers could measure its tiny movements when hit by a gas particle. The resulting impulses were as small as a billionth of a Newton acting for one ten-trillionth of a second. And the rate of the collisions grew as the researchers introduced more gas into the chamber, increasing the pressure within.
That suggests a possible application for the technique. “This could enable a very good way to sense pressure,” says physicist Yu-Han Tseng of Yale University, especially at very low pressures — such as in space or in vacuum chambers. The system could also distinguish between the different types of gases Tseng and colleagues studied, as each one interacted differently with the nanoparticle.
A device like this could help reveal the composition of particles in space, and even on other worlds, Tseng says. “You can imagine putting it on another planet and [using] that to study the environment there.”

Vincent van Gogh’s “The Starry Night” may have been based on one specific night sky: July 22, 1889, just before dawn over France.
If that’s true, it means the famous painting was based on real observations, not just van Gogh’s imagination, astronomer Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim and colleagues report October 22 in Scientific Reports.
“How could an invented sky fit the sky of a particular date this closely?” the team writes. “Observation and imagination have commonly been treated as an either/or, yet ‘The Starry Night’ shows the two coexisting on one canvas.”
Art historians typically date “The Starry Night” to mid-June 1889, based on one of van Gogh’s letters to his brother Theo.
“At last I have a landscape with olive trees, and also a new study of a starry sky,” van Gogh wrote on or about June 18. About a month earlier, van Gogh had entered a hospital in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, France. “The Starry Night” is thought to represent the view through the window of his room. A short time later, van Gogh experienced an illness during which he didn’t paint for about six weeks, so most historians think “The Starry Night” must have been painted before then.
That letter is taken as strong evidence, says astronomer Donald Olson of Texas State University in San Marcos, who has written about how astronomy shows up in art history. Historians favor the June date because “van Gogh himself said so,” he says.
That assumption has led to some confusion, though. In the 1980s, two astronomers tried to match the painting’s stars to real skies in Saint-Rémy in mid-June. One proposed that the sky was from June 19, 1889, and the collection of swirly stars is the constellation Aries.
But the other concluded it couldn’t have been painted on June 19, based on cloudy weather reports in Aix-en-Provence, France, about 70 kilometers away. That study claimed the painting was “a celestial composite, constructed to make an image of the morning sky.”
Kim, who founded a telescope-building company called SLLAB Inc. in Seoul, South Korea, didn’t know about the June date when he became interested in “The Starry Night.” “Unlike previous astronomical studies, we could start freely,” he says.
Given his job, Kim had an intuition for which stars would be visible when. “People like me, who guide a telescope through its first alignment with the sky, naturally memorize where the stars are,” he says.
He was skeptical of the Aries theory. The stars in that constellation are faint enough that they wouldn’t be all that visible in the predawn sky, “hardly enough to inspire a painter,” he says.
Instead, Kim saw the stars as the Hyades star cluster, which forms a sideways V shape in the constellation Taurus. To test that theory, he and his colleagues applied a statistical technique called Procrustes shape analysis to put a number to how well the stars in the painting matched any particular constellation.
Celestial alignment?
Researchers compared the V-shaped collection of stars in “The Starry Night” (first image) with those in the Hyades star cluster (middle image). The resulting graph (last image) maps the real stars (blue) and the painting’s stars (orange) against each other. They don’t overlap perfectly, but they’re suspiciously close, researchers say. The label Sn stands for “The Starry Night.” while the constellation’s Greek letters represent typical astronomy notation.
E.J. Kim et al./Scientific Reports, 2026
E.J. Kim et al./Scientific Reports, 2026
E.J. Kim et al./Scientific Reports, 2026
The team tested the method on another van Gogh skyscape, “Starry Night Over the Rhône,” which clearly depicts the Big Dipper. “Apart from the Big Dipper, there is no star pattern we can say for certain that Vincent painted,” Kim says. The degree of matching between the art and the sky for both paintings turned out to be similar, a major clue.
Kim also used the position and phase of the moon (a waxing gibbous on June 19, in contrast to the sharp waning crescent in the painting) and Venus to further constrain the painting’s date. He used computer simulations that weren’t available in the ‘80s to calculate the positions of celestial objects on certain dates in 1889 down to the second. He even traveled to France in June and July 2019 to try to find the field of view van Gogh would have seen from his window. Ultimately, July 22, 1889, was the best fit for the team’s data.
“I still cannot forget the moment we finally found the spot, overlaid the drawing on the view and saw it fit perfectly,” Kim says. “I was standing where Vincent had stood 130 years earlier. And the thrill I felt when I confirmed that the moon, the Hyades and Venus of July 22, 1889, fit exactly within the drawing’s field of view is still with me.”
Not to douse Kim’s enthusiasm, but that field of view may not be exactly what van Gogh saw, Olson says.
“The authors’ assumed narrow field of view, essential for their theory that the stars of the Hyades fill most of the canvas, is inconsistent with the much wider field of view required to encompass ‘The Starry Night’s’ round hills and cliffs,” he says. That casts doubt on the paper’s conclusions.
Olson proposes an experiment: Tell an amateur astronomer that “The Starry Night” depicts the Hyades and ask them to point out the star Aldebaran, which is at the bottom left of the V. In real life, this is the brightest star in the Hyades. But the painting has other much more prominent stars.

Two months before the treatment that would change Lynn Montgomery-Haga’s life, she could barely walk down a hallway.
In a test at the University of Colorado Anschutz, Montgomery-Haga struggled to walk 25 feet, often reaching out to the walls for support. Usually, the 49-year-old relied on her walker or wheelchair. “She had a very stiff, hesitant gait,” says Montgomery-Haga’s neurologist, Amanda Piquet.
For about a decade, Montgomery-Haga had lived with a debilitating autoimmune disease known as stiff person syndrome. The progressive condition can lock up the body’s muscles without warning, leading to falls, broken bones, excruciating pain and difficulty moving. Singer Celine Dion, who returned to the stage in September after years of battling the disease, has said it can feel “like somebody’s strangling you.”
Montgomery-Haga’s own days were marked by dizziness, fatigue and pain. And sudden muscle spasms would send her sprawling. It was like the fainting goat videos popular on the internet, she says. “They get surprised and they fall over, and there’s nothing they can do about it.”
But stiff person syndrome is no joke. It stripped Montgomery-Haga of her accounting job and her ability to drive. She couldn’t sit up in bed unless she had a safety bar to pull on. If she dropped the soap in the shower, it’d take her 10 minutes to pick it up.
Now, Montgomery-Haga hopes those struggles are finally coming to an end. That’s because a clinical trial with an experimental therapy has helped restore mobility for her — and others like her. She can stride through her living room again. She can landscape her front yard. She doesn’t have to brace herself when her dogs jump on her. And she hasn’t fallen once since the treatment. The change has been drastic, she says. “I’m just really excited about the future.”
One day, Montgomery-Haga hopes she’s able to walk all three of her dogs (Henley Rose, Smoky Joe and Lacey Mae, from left to right) at the same time.AAron Ontiveroz
The treatment, a type of CAR T cell therapy, extracts immune cells from a person’s body and engineers them to attack the very cells causing the disease. First used to fight cancer, CAR T is now also targeting a variety of autoimmune diseases. If given the green light by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Montgomery-Haga’s treatment would be the first such therapy approved for an autoimmune condition — and it would be the first approved treatment for stiff person syndrome.
Stiff person syndrome may be just the beginning, says Carl June, the University of Pennsylvania immunologist and oncologist who spearheaded CAR T cell therapy for cancer decades ago. The “living drug” could herald a new era of therapeutics for autoimmune diseases like lupus, rheumatoid arthritis and even multiple sclerosis. “It’s revolutionary to think how far things have gone,” June says.
But he warns that it’s far too early to know if scientists have definitively cured stiff person syndrome. And there haven’t been enough people treated to get a good handle on all the possible side effects. “There could be long-term complications in autoimmune patients that don’t happen in our cancer patients,” he says. Other researchers urge caution. “It’s very important not to oversell it,” says Marc Scherlinger, a rheumatologist at Strasbourg University Hospital in France.
For Piquet, one crucial question is how long the treatment will last. In Montgomery-Haga’s case, the answer seems to be at least two years. Montgomery-Haga still considers herself disabled, or “disabled-ish,” as she calls it. But when rating how she used to feel on a scale of one to 10, she’d put herself at a zero before treatment, she says. These days, she’s more like a seven.
What’s more, Montgomery-Haga says, “I think I’m still improving.”
At 40, Lynn Montgomery-Haga was diagnosed with stiff person syndrome, a rare autoimmune disease that can cause severe muscle spasms and rigidity. In 2024, she received an experimental CAR T cell therapy for her condition — then her mobility began to come back.Animations by Eric Pio; Edited by Damien S. Alipour; Produced by Mandana Tadayon
No approved therapies
There’s no single symptom that clued Montgomery-Haga in to her disease. In 2014, she started having difficulty picking things up off the floor. Then her boss asked her why she was limping — Montgomery-Haga hadn’t noticed. Her balance was off and her head felt weird, like “I was walking around in a fishbowl,” she says. It got to the point where Montgomery-Haga had difficulty crossing thresholds between rooms.
Montgomery-Haga would startle easily, prompting her body to stiffen up like a board. One time when cooking, she burned her finger, spasmed and collapsed, cracking the back of her head on the cabinets. She lay on the floor crying, but finally managed to right herself. “As soon as you hit the floor,” she says, “your muscles are like, ‘Fine,’ and you can get up again.”
Those unpredictable symptoms capture a slice of what life is like with stiff person syndrome, or SPS. The disease, which affects roughly 2 in 100,000 people in the United States, typically develops in a person’s 30s or 40s. It is about twice as common in women as in men.
Scientists don’t know what sets off the disease. But they think a person’s own antibodies start attacking a neurological network that helps muscles throughout the body relax. And when those tensed muscles are in opposition, like the biceps and triceps, they s

Scientific papers may be getting a 21st century update.
A system called Paper2Agent lets scientists do more than read a new scientific study. When a paper comes with code, methods and data, the system packages these into a tool set that an AI assistant can use to work with new data, researchers report September 16 in Nature.
The system is essentially “a virtual author of the paper,” available around the clock, says James Zou, a computer scientist at Stanford University.
In tests, Zou and colleagues tried to convert 100 computational biology papers into working tool sets and succeeded with 74. The others had obstacles such as missing code or data, or software that wouldn’t run. With the papers that were converted, the Paper2Agent tool set could run analyses of the published work and answer questions about the results. It did so more accurately and also more than twice as fast as the same agent working from the original papers and accompanying code.
Making another scientist’s code usable can take substantial work, says Peter Clark, a senior research director at the Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence in Seattle who was not involved in developing Paper2Agent. Researchers already share code on platforms such as GitHub. But Clark says he often has to “grub around” for half a day to figure out how to get it running.
A general-purpose AI assistant such as Claude can help, he says, but it typically generates new code on the fly. Paper2Agent instead packages code associated with a paper into reusable tools, tests them against reference outputs and writes step-by-step instructions guiding an AI assistant on which tools to use and in what order. This streamlines and standardizes the process of using AI to interact with scientific research, Clark says. It’s “an exciting step” toward papers that actively help scientists.
To Zou, transforming scientific papers into agents seem like a natural next step for transmitting knowledge. We’ve already moved from stone tablets and papyrus to paper and then to digital formats, he says, and now it’s time to move from passive to active formats for human knowledge. A paper-agent can help one human scientist quickly use another’s code and methods. The tool can also search for paper-agents about similar topics with the aim of alerting their human authors about potential collaborations.
Zou says his team has already created “over 100 different paper-agents” from their own work and that these have already helped him find other scientists to collaborate with.
Clark notes that Paper2Agent specializes in helping scientists reuse methods and code, and not in answering general questions, like a true virtual author should be able to do. Also, he worries about what could happen if millions of low-quality papers get turned into agents capable of pestering scientists. That could make things “worse rather than better,” he says, recalling the days of Clippy, the much-maligned Microsoft Office assistant. But he’d love for a “non-annoying agent” to pop up and tell him about work that he should be paying attention to.
For more open-ended questions about a paper, Clark says he would still want to talk to the people who did the research. “The reason I would write to a corresponding author is for precisely the things they didn’t put in the paper.”

Cartwheeling seems like it should require both arms and legs. But some itty-bitty snakes in Southeast Asia manage it without either.
Scientists first shared snapshots of a dwarf reed snake (Pseudorabdion longiceps) cartwheeling away from danger in 2023. Now, videos of three Pseudorabdion species hightailing it down a racetrack in the lab have offered a closer look at this rare and strangely acrobatic behavior.
Each snake starts with its body curled into a C shape, head lifted off the ground and facing the way it’s going. It then whips its tail out behind it, briefly becoming airborne. The snake flips its tail forward and down past its head. When the snake’s tail hits the ground in front of it, another roll begins, researchers report October 19 in Current Biology.
“What a cool snake behavior,” says Jessica Tingle, a biologist at Brown University in Providence, R.I., not involved in the work. “I find it especially amazing that an elongate animal like a snake can manage to roll, especially given that they do it in such an explosive way, which probably asks a lot of their muscles and bones.”
Watch a Pseudorabdion saravacense cartwheel down a racetrack in the lab. Videos like this helped researchers pinpoint how these snakes perform their gymnastics. Y. Kojima et al./Current Biology 2026
Yosuke Kojima was equally surprised when a colleague in Sarawak, Malaysia recounted witnessing this “very weird” behavior in 2019. So the researchers collected snakes from Malaysia’s Kubah National Park. They scooped up 11 P. saravacense, one P. collaris, one P. longiceps, plus six Calamaria reed snakes for comparison.
Finding the snakes was no easy task. They were only about 11 to 28 centimeters long. “They always hide under the leaves,” says Kojima, an ecologist at Toho University in Chiba, Japan. But were any of the snakes able to cartwheel away from the researchers? “No,” Kojima laughs. “We are quicker than them.”
The team set up a 2.2-meter-long racetrack and placed the snakes one at a time at one end. A gentle tap coaxed the snakes to move and cameras above and beside the track recorded the action. None of the Calamaria snakes cartwheeled, but all of the Pseudorabdion snakes did. At full tilt, they tumbled at 1.7 to 3.7 meters per second — about six to 13 kilometers per hour.
Through it all, the snakes held their heads fairly steady — reminiscent of how flying snakes hold their heads stable while launching into the air, the researchers say.
Round and round
A cartwheeling snake first rolls its body along the ground to whip its tail out behind its head. Then, it swings its tail up and over its head. Finally, it brings its tail down on either the left or right side of its head. Once it the tail hits the ground, the snake is ready for another roll. In the cartwheel seen on top, the snake brings its tail down on the left side of its head, angling its whitish belly toward the viewer. In the cartwheel on the bottom, the snake’s tail lands on the right side of its head, showing its darker back to the viewer.
Yosuke Kojima, Kanon Tanaka
“I am very curious how such a strange and possibly demanding movement evolved … whether dwarf reed snakes have something special in their anatomy, physiology or neural control that lets them do it when their close relatives apparently can’t or don’t,” Tingle says. “Are their brains different in some way to let them coordinate a fast and unusual movement? Or do all snakes have the basic equipment, and they just don’t use it?”
Those may be open mysteries. But catching snakes cartwheeling on camera does tie up one loose end for Tingle.
“Some writers in the 1800s talked about ‘hoop snakes’ and described their motion as rolling, but that seemed pretty fantastical to me, and I chalked it up to overly inventive imaginations,” Tingle says. Those 19th century authors may or may not have been describing the exact behavior Kojima’s team recorded. “Either way, it’s neat to find out a real animal does something reminiscent of a fantastical old story.”
